timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Open access brings opens the flood gates of access to knowledge.
And what sets stake a lot because in the realm specifically of scientific information,
access is so restricted because journals are so expensive, especially in developing
countries which have health challenges, environmental challenges.
So a lot of the information is actually most critical to these developing countries,
but unfortunately they don't have access to it.
So I think what sets stake is in development and sustainable development.
I'm Indrajit Banerjee and I'm the director of the Knowledge Society's Dimission of UNESCO.
Actually, UNESCO's mission is a perfect fit for of access because one of our core mandates
is to promote free flow of ideas by word, by image.
You can't have free flow of ideas if people don't have access.
So it's just a perfect fit for us.
You see, one of the things is that when we try and we are a member states-based organization,
we are 195 member countries.
And when we try to do any projects on open access, very often the question is, what's
this good for?
And then you explain to them why it's good.
And when they get convinced, they say, OK, how do we do it?
And we've noticed that there are so many policy obstacles and policy challenges to open
access.
That the perhaps the starting point in this case would be to create a policy framework
and guidelines, which we can then share with our member states.
And once our member states have that, then often they call us and say, can you come into
a workshop for our Ministry of Education officials or education people, teachers so that they
understand what this whole question of open access is all about.
So I think the policy guidelines are a very good starting point because it also makes
them understand it better.
They have concrete product in their hands.
They can pass legislation if required, as has happened in many countries, of course.
So I think the policy guidelines was a very important step, but I would like to add that
the policy guidelines were a result of a global mapping we had done on open access.
We had to have some sense of where open access stands.
So we did a global mapping.
We have a portal called Global Open Access Portal, which has got, for the moment, I think
it's got data on 148 countries.
And they clearly saw that there were some countries where it was a huge success because
there was a policy environment.
There was a political will.
And other countries where it had not really moved very much.
So the policy guidelines were the second step.

youtube_description: Indrajit Banerjee, Director of the Knowledge Societies Division of UNESCO, explains that open access fits perfectly into UNESCO's mission "to promote the free flow of ideas by word and by image": ideas can't flow freely if people don't have access, he says. In this interview, he explains what's at stake for developing countries, especially, and how UNESCO's guidelines are a concrete first step.
